newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy govt calls confidence vote, opposition angry.
newsitem.headline: Italy govt calls confidence vote, opposition angry.

text.p: Italy's centre-left government on Monday called a confidence vote in the lower house of parliament to speed up approval of its controversial mini-budget in a move bitterly condemned by opposition parties.

Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi announced the step in the Chamber of Deputies after a cabinet decision to put the mini-budget, vital to Italy's hopes of joining Europe's single currency, to a test of confidence.
It will be the 21st such do-or-die vote since Prime Minister Romano Prodi took office a year ago.
The timing of the vote, which Prodi was expected to win, was not immediately decided but at least 24 hours have to elapse before it can be held under parliamentary rules.

Hard right National Alliance party leader Gianfranco Fini, a key figure in the main opposition Freedom Alliance bloc, called the decision intolerable. "The Prodi government is preventing parliament from discussing and possibly amending the government's measures," he said.

The 1997 mini-budget is designed to cut 15.5 trillion lire ($9.1 billion) from this year's deficit in a bid to meet tough criteria laid down in the Maastricht Treaty for founder membership of the planned euro currency at its launch in 1999.
The package has been lambasted by the opposition and even by centrists within Prodi's own coalition for demanding early payment of taxes by companies on severance payment funds.

Diego Masi, a member of the small, pro-government Patto Segni group, pledged support for Prodi in the vote but remarked that the government had "put a pistol to our heads" by making the package a confidence issue.

Ciampi initially sought six trillion lire from the anticipated taxes on severance funds but agreed, in the face of widespread discontent, to reduce this to five trillion and make up the difference with the help of tax amnesties.
However the cut was not enough for many parliamentarians and the budget committee rejected the proposed mini-budget last month after two centre-left deputies broke government ranks.

The hard-left Communist Refoundation, which secures Prodi's majority in the lower house, voted with the government and budget rebels in the committee indicated they would back the coalition if the budget was put to a confidence test.
The cabinet decided to call a confidence vote at a meeting on Monday in the light of hundreds of amendments pinned to the package by the opposition.

Victory for Prodi on the confidence motion will sweep away proposed changes, allowing the bill to move to the Senate (upper house). Under Italian law, both houses must approve the budget before the end of May or else it would be scrapped.
The Freedom Alliance staged a mass demonstration at the weekend in Milan to protest against the government and its economic record.

Prodi has introduced just under 100 trillion lire of belt-tightening measures over the past year as he fights to lower the budget deficit to three percent of Gross Domestic Product, as demanded by the Maastricht Treaty for single currency aspirants. The ratio was 6.7 percent in 1996.
